newsitem.title: USA: CIA grapples with scoundrel policy fallout.
newsitem.headline: CIA grapples with scoundrel policy fallout.

text.p: The Central Intelligence Agency has been in a quandary over just how dastardly the spies it recruits abroad may be.

The issue has opened CIA Director John Deutch to an election-year attack from Republicans who accuse him of currying favour with liberals at the expense of keeping tabs on terrorists, drug runners and other criminal gangs.
The problem was posed in stark terms last month by a Pentagon task force on the guerrilla bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, on June 25.

Although U.S. intelligence had long before named the site, Khobar Towers, as a likely terrorist target, details on how and when the attack would take place were lacking, the task force said in its Sept. 16 report.

"The United States must invest more time, effort and resources into developing these crucial sources of information," the report said. "Moreover, policy restrictions on recruitment of sources may hamper the efforts of national intelligence agencies and must be re-examined."
House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, seeming to play off the task force's slap at Deutch over recruitment, called two days later for a post-election probe of the CIA.

"The degree to which it has been politicized should be ripped apart and we should insist on the establishment of a professional Central Intelligence Agency with a professional director dedicated to the defence of the United States rather than to the defence of left-wing politicians," the Georgia Republican, said on Sept. 18 in accepting an award from the Centre for Security Policy, a public policy group.

In recent weeks Deutch has been at pains to defend his recruitment rules, which require case officers to get a green light from headquarters before doing business with "unsavory characters" such as criminals with blood on their hands.

"The rules we have put in place reflect higher standards for tradecraft, agent validation and counterintelligence," Deutch said in a Sept. 5 speech crafted in part to respond to Republican criticism that the Clinton administration had let its guard down against terrorists.
He added that the CIA had "substantially increased the number of new sources reporting to us about terrorist groups" in the past 18 months.

Deutch announced his new recruitment rules on Sept. 29, 1995, in response to disclosures that the CIA had paid $44,000 to a Guatemalan colonel implicated in the murder and torture of a U.S. innkeeper and a Guatemalan guerrilla leader married to a U.S. citizen.
Despite the new rules, no would-be CIA "asset" has been turned down at headquarters level because of a checkered past, Deutch told the House Intelligence Committee on Sept. 25.
He admitted CIA case officers continued to wrestle with the issue, saying it came up at each of 32 overseas stations he had toured since taking over as U.S. spymaster in May 1995.

"In each instance, this issue is raised and discussed fully," he said. On the key matter of whether the rules caused any CIA officers to shrink from a perceived risk of sending up troublesome names, he said he was trying to combat any such misconception.

Steven Aftergood, an intelligence policy critic who edits the Federation of American Scientists' Secrecy & Government Bulletin, said one way for the CIA to clear the air would be to make its guidelines public. "Historically, the best intelligence sources have been noble volunteers, not sleazeballs," he added.

Asked about releasing the guidelines, which are internal and classified, CIA spokeman Mark Mansfield said the spies who need to work under them "know them well." But Deutch would go on explaining them in congressional testimony and other public appearances, he added.
